Title: Takt time expresses customer pace; kanban limits authorized replenishment
Caption: Separate assigned examples: daily demand determines takt; kanban calculation uses30 units/h, replenishment lead time2 h,10 units/container, and10% allowance on expected lead-time demand. Takt is not actual cycle time. Seven containers authorize70 units in the illustrated loop; card count depends on replenishment reliability and the defined boundary.

Title: PDCA and DMAIC organize improvement around measurement and feedback
Caption: Conceptual comparison of improvement cycles. PDCA checks a change against its prediction; DMAIC emphasizes problem definition, baseline measurement, cause analysis, improvement, and sustained control. Stage labels alone do not establish causation or statistical validity. Neither cycle requires accepting a change that harms other constraints.

Title: Value engineering compares function and lifecycle cost before selecting an alternative
Caption: Assigned function scores and lifecycle costs with one consistent boundary. Alternative B has85/90=0.944 score points per$1000 versus80/100=0.8 for A. A scoring scale must be justified; this is an illustrative comparison, not a procurement recommendation. Reliability, safety, service, and other mandatory requirements are screened before ratios.

Title: Resource efficiency accounts for useful output and residual streams on the same basis
Caption: Assigned steady mass balance without reaction or accumulation. Recovered material is an external exit, not both an exit and an uncounted internal recycle. Product yield is80%; product plus recovery totals95% diverted from the unrecovered stream but is not95% product yield. Energy, water, toxicity, and lifecycle effects require separate indicators.

Title: Improvement validation checks the entire system against a comparable baseline
Caption: Assigned before/after observations illustrate a nonconstraint improvement that adds release pressure. They are not a controlled experiment and cannot establish cause by themselves. Verify comparable mix, demand, staffing, quality, and system boundary; estimate uncertainty and watch for displaced bottlenecks or queues before claiming a system benefit.

Title: From-to flows and a distance matrix give a transparent load-distance score
Caption: Assigned flows and coordinates, with Manhattan distance and no obstacles. Score contributions are30+35+6+32+4=107 load·m/day. Loads are a common unit across links; no monetary handling rate or travel-time penalty is assigned. Symmetric distances do not imply symmetric flows, and this single layout has not been optimized.

Title: The same endpoints have different distances under different movement rules
Caption: Coordinates A(0,0), B(3,4) m. Euclidean is straight physical path length; rectilinear uses separate axis travel. Chebyshev corresponds to simultaneous axis motion with equal speed limits and a time-equivalent distance, not the Euclidean length of the dashed path. Obstacles and unequal axis speeds require a different model.

Title: Layout types organize flow around sequence, function, product families, or a stationary product
Caption: Four conceptual layouts, not to scale. Product layouts follow a repeated route; process layouts group similar functions; cells combine operations for a product family; fixed-position layouts bring resources to a stationary product. Real layouts must also account for access, safety, buffers, utilities, and changing mix.

Title: Discrete plant location balances fixed opening cost with customer service cost
Caption: Fixed cost$40 per open site. Matrix rows are customers and columns are sites; entries cover each customer’s complete demand over one common period. Each customer is assigned once to an open site. No site capacities or distance restrictions are imposed, so all nonempty opening patterns can be enumerated. The tie is intentional, not a unique location recommendation.

Title: Machine requirements compare processing workload with usable time per machine
Caption: Assigned identical compatible machines, one product unit at a time, processing times include the stated work content. Usable420 minutes already excludes planned unavailable time; do not subtract the same loss again. Ceiling gives an aggregate capacity requirement, not a guaranteed schedule. Setups, yields, batching, and routing can increase the practical requirement.

Title: Crew requirements use standard labor content and available crew time
Caption: Assigned work content is elapsed standard time for an entire two-person crew, not person-minutes. Two crews correspond to four people under that composition. Available time must use an allowance convention consistent with the standard times, avoiding duplicate deductions. Aggregate rounding does not establish skill coverage, shift balance, or schedulability.

Title: Material-handling selection matches load and route characteristics to equipment capabilities
Caption: Qualitative selection matrix, not equipment sizing or purchasing advice. Capability depends on actual dimensions, center of gravity, floor/route conditions, traffic, and controls. A material-handling metric can combine distance and loads but does not capture all congestion, maintenance, labor, or safety effects.

Title: Supply chains carry material, information, and payment in distinct directions
Caption: Conceptual chain. Material generally moves toward customers, while returns can move upstream. Demand and shipment information can be shared both ways; settlement typically flows upstream but actual contracts can differ. Arrows represent flow types rather than time or volume. End-to-end service depends on coordinated capacities, lead times, and inventories.

Title: Transportation allocation minimizes cost while meeting every supply and demand balance
Caption: Balanced assigned transportation model with divisible units, no route capacities or fixed charges. Every row shipment equals its supply and every column receipt meets demand. The plan has cost115 and was verified by linear programming; equal-cost alternate allocations can exist. Allocation fractions do not imply that indivisible loads can be split without an integer model.

Title: Network design separates facility-opening decisions from subsequent shipment allocation
Caption: Conceptual capacitated facility-location formulation. qij is shipment from site j to customer i; Kj is capacity over the same period as customer demand, and fj is its fixed opening cost. The linking constraint prohibits shipment from a closed site. Time/service constraints need explicit modeling. No network solution or capacity values are assigned.

Title: Risk pooling depends on demand covariance, not simply the number of locations
Caption: Assigned jointly normal lead-time demands, equal lead-time windows, same z service factor, and no extra pooling delays. Pooling replaces two stocks with one stock against the combined demand. At correlation1 the statistical benefit disappears. Separate location cycle-service probabilities and pooled system cycle-service probability do not define the same fill-rate or joint-service event.

Title: Multiechelon distribution places inventories between successive replenishment stages
Caption: Conceptual two-warehouse-echelon network after the plant. Local installation inventory and echelon inventory have different boundaries: echelon stock includes specified downstream stock and transit. Allocation, replenishment, transit times, and shortages interact across levels; independent local safety- stock optimization need not be a system optimum.

Title: Lead-time uncertainty and disruption recovery affect service through different mechanisms
Caption: Assigned normal lead-time-demand distributions illustrate variability at a fixed reorder point. They are not measured supplier lead-time data; cycle- service probability is not order fill rate. Rare disruptions may lie outside a normal model. Alternate supply, recovery time, visibility, and protected capacity require separate service and cost evaluation.

Title: The bullwhip effect describes amplification of order variability upstream
Caption: Synthetic aligned sequences with deviations multiplied by2 and3, giving variance ratios4 and9 exactly. No causal replenishment simulation is claimed. Batching, forecasts, delays, incentives, and shortages can amplify orders in actual systems. Coordination may reduce amplification, but its effect needs comparable measured variability and service outcomes.

Title: Usable controls expose system state and make action consequences observable
Caption: Conceptual human-system interaction loop. Control-display mapping, legibility, consistency, feedback timing, and recoverable errors affect usability. Assigned measures are proposed evaluation dimensions, not test results. Workload is not inferred from completion time alone. A display should communicate actionable state without assuming color is the only distinguishable cue.

Title: Percentile design treats reach, clearance, and adjustability as different requirements
Caption: Assigned normal dimension gives5th≈51.78 cm and95th≈68.22 cm. These are not anthropometric measurements of an actual population. A reach limit typically considers smaller users; clearance considers larger dimensions. Percentile coverage is dimension-specific and cannot be combined into a universal “5th- percentile person.” Clothing, posture, task, and population change requirements.

Title: External load moment increases with perpendicular reach distance
Caption: Elementary external static moment model around a reference joint, with force perpendicular to the moment arm. It excludes body-segment weights, muscle lever arms, dynamics, and internal joint forces, so it is not a lifting limit or injury prediction. Cumulative exposure also depends on repetition, duration, posture, and recovery; no numeric trauma threshold is asserted.

Title: Noise dose adds exposure fractions under the stated exchange-rate convention
Caption: Illustrative U.S. OSHA general-industry Appendix A computation: assigned segments only, with no additional counted noise. This dose model uses a5 dB exchange rate, not equal-energy3 dB averaging. Actual exposure assessment needs calibrated measurements, correct integration settings, and the full workshift. Dose arithmetic alone is not a determination of safe exposure or compliance.

Title: Methods analysis separates useful handling from repeated searching and travel
Caption: Conceptual method redesign with a defined tool location and reduced retrieval. No measured time saving is assigned. A method study documents the operation, analyzes motions, develops a feasible method, then evaluates quality, reach, force, repetition, and worker feedback. Fewer steps can shift effort or strain and must be verified rather than assumed beneficial.

Title: Standard time depends on the rating and on how the allowance fraction is defined
Caption: Assigned cycles and rating for one repeatable task. A rating above100% normalizes a faster-than-standard observed performance upward. The two allowance conventions are alternatives, not cumulative adjustments:15% of normal job time differs from15% of the workday. Sampling adequacy, outlier treatment, task method, and allowance basis must be established for actual standards.

Title: Work sampling estimates an activity fraction; a unit learning curve models repetition time
Caption: Independent random work-sampling snapshots, binary classification, and a normal interval are assumed; correlated or biased observations invalidate this simple interval. The separate assigned80% unit-time learning curve reduces time to80% at each doubling. It is not the cumulative-average model, and does not prove a person will follow that curve. No link between the two example datasets is implied.

Title: Quality planning, assurance, control, and improvement have distinct purposes
Caption: Conceptual quality-management structure. Planning defines acceptable outcomes and methods; assurance examines the process and evidence; control evaluates realized results; improvement changes causes and verifies effects. These roles interact rather than form a mandatory linear certification sequence. Proposed metrics include defect rate, first-pass yield, and recurrence of validated nonconformities.

Title: A house of quality translates customer priorities into technical response priorities
Caption: Assigned two-need, three-response QFD matrix. Weighted scores are5×[9,1,3]+3×[1,9,1]=[48,32,18], with no implied engineering units. Roof signs illustrate interactions between improvement directions, not measured correlations. This simplified house omits benchmarking, targets, and difficulty ratings; scores inform discussion but do not override feasibility or mandatory requirements.

Title: Cause-and-effect analysis proposes hypotheses; Taguchi loss quantifies deviation from target
Caption: Original fishbone branches list candidate causes, not demonstrated causal relationships. Assigned quadratic loss uses target10 mm and calibration$4 at0.2 mm deviation, giving$1 at0.1 mm. The curve expresses a teaching economic model and does not define specification limits, actual warranty cost, or the probability of a defect.

Title: An X-bar chart monitors subgroup means against control limits, not specification limits
Caption: Assigned subgroup means with known stable baseline mean10 mm and within-process SD0.08 mm. Limits apply to subgroup means, not individual parts. One beyond-limit point triggers investigation under the stated rule, not proof of a specific cause. Specifications are intentionally absent. A chart alone does not certify capability or establish its own valid baseline.

Title: Cp measures potential spread capability; Cpk also accounts for centering
Caption: Assigned stable normal populations, identical within-process SD and specification limits9.7–10.3 mm. Shifting the mean leaves Cp unchanged while lowering Cpk. These are population examples rather than estimated sample indices; uncertainty, nonnormality, instability, and measurement-system effects require separate evaluation. A single threshold is not presented as a universal acceptance rule.

Title: An OC curve shows the probability of accepting a lot at each defect fraction
Caption: Assigned single-sampling binomial model, large lot or negligible sampling fraction, independent identically distributed defect classifications. At illustrative good qualityp=.01 producer rejection risk isα; at poor qualityp=.10 consumer acceptance risk isβ. These points are assigned, not an adopted standard plan. Finite-lot sampling without replacement can require a hypergeometric OC curve.

Title: A factorial experiment estimates main effects and interaction with replicated error
Caption: Assigned full two-level factorial with two observations per cell and coded factors±1. Interaction creates nonparallel mean lines; effects are high-minus- low contrasts and differ from regression coefficients by a factor of two. ANOVA partitions120 response-units² into32+72+8+8. Randomization, independent constant-variance errors, and residual checks are needed for inferential use; no causal field experiment is claimed.
